sentences.text: Unlike more derived relatives, Aetosaurus possessed a long, narrow carapace that lacked spikes. The paramedian scutes covering its back were considerably wider than they were long, while the lateral scutes bore no projections. This armored shell was notably "waisted," meaning it narrowed significantly in front of the pelvis.

The genus was first named and described in 1877 by the German paleontologist Oscar Fraas. At that time, the species was known from twenty-two articulated skeletons found in the Lower Stubensandstein of Germany.
Thirty years after the initial description, Eberhard Fraas described the second species, A. crassicauda, also from Germany.
In 1896, Othniel Charles Marsh named Stegomus arcuatus based on a cast of an aetosaur known as YPM 1647 from the New Haven Formation. In 1998, the genus Stegomus was synonymized with Aetosaurus.
Aetosaurus belongs to the family Stagonolepididae and the subfamily Aetosaurinae.
Three species are currently recognized: A. ferratus from Germany and Italy, A. crassicauda from Germany, and A. arcuatus from eastern North America.
Specimens of Aetosaurus occur in strata dating to the Norian age. The animal lived between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago during the Norian stage.
